issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Exposed to Others' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure in this profile. It implies a visible, externally legible stigma or mark of trauma, but the rest of the profile does not include appearance-related injury, shame, or social-evaluative threat that would make this appraisal clinically coherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is not impossible after a toxic exposure, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation because no other item suggests a preventable omission, responsibility for others, or a scenario where the patient had a realistic chance to stop the event. In this profile it reads as insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is a weak fit to the trauma type and to the rest of the selected items. Loud or unexpected sounds are not a natural trigger/threat cue for toxic chemical exposure unless the trauma involved explosions, alarms, or similarly salient auditory signals, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a 76-year-old male with trauma from toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' is the least coherent item in the profile. Toxic chemical exposure more plausibly yields themes of bodily damage, contamination, helplessness, or mistrust of the body/environment. Severe guilt about not preventing the event can occur, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile: there are no memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting a role in causing the incident, failing to rescue others, or making a consequential decision. The other appraisal items are strongly body-focused and fit the trauma type well, making this guilt item stand out as insufficiently integrated with the formulation and surrounding content. The remaining items are clinically coherent with one another and with the active formulation pattern, especially the strong links among memory, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies.

vignette:
Richard, a seventy-six-year-old hotel manager, had spent forty years overseeing a mid-sized downtown property, priding himself on anticipating problems before they arose. Nothing, however, had prepared him for the morning a maintenance worker improperly mixed cleaning solvents in a basement storage closet, releasing a cloud of acrid, chemical fumes that traveled up through the ventilation system. Richard had been in his first-floor office when the smell hit—sharp, sweet, and burning all at once. He remembered the way his throat closed, the searing in his lungs, the frantic scramble to evacuate guests while his own vision swam. He had not lost consciousness, but he had felt, for several minutes, that he might die right there in the lobby, gasping for air that only made things worse.

In the weeks that followed, Richard noticed that his memory of that morning did not come as a single, clear story. Instead, it arrived in fragments: the fluorescent lights flickering overhead, the sound of a woman screaming somewhere behind him, the weight of a guest’s suitcase he had grabbed without thinking. These pieces did not fit together in any logical order, and sometimes he would be standing in his kitchen at home and suddenly feel the full, crushing terror of that moment—his heart hammering, his chest tight—without any image or thought to explain why. What disturbed him most was the smell. At odd times, with no warning, he would catch the faint odor of bleach and ammonia, as if it were seeping through the walls of his own apartment, and he would freeze, certain that he was about to be poisoned again.

Richard had come to believe that his body had betrayed him. He could no longer trust it to keep him safe. His hands would tremble at the grocery store when a child dropped a jar on the floor, and his lungs would seize up at the sound of a truck backfiring outside his window. He was certain, with a conviction that felt unshakable, that his body kept reacting as if he were still in that basement hallway, even when he was perfectly safe. He had begun to think of his own nervous system as an enemy, something that would not listen to reason. And this terrified him more than the event itself, because it meant that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. He felt helpless in a way he had never felt before, not even during his divorce.

To manage this constant sense of threat, Richard had developed a set of habits that now governed his daily life. He had not set foot in the hotel since the incident, and he had called in sick so many times that his assistant manager had gently suggested he take a formal leave of absence. Richard had agreed, but the absence of work left him with too much time to sit and monitor his own thoughts, scanning them for signs that he was losing his mind. He would catch himself thinking, "That's a crazy thought," and then spiral into worry that he was on the verge of a breakdown. At home, he kept the television or a loud radio playing constantly, not for entertainment but to drown out the small, unexpected sounds that made him jump—the creak of a floorboard, the hum of the refrigerator, the distant siren that could have been an ambulance or could have been anything.

He had come to feel safe in only a very limited number of places: his own bedroom, with the door closed and the windows locked, and a single chair in his living room that faced the front door. Everywhere else felt exposed. Even inside his own home, he was on high alert, listening for footsteps in the hallway, for the sound of the building's ventilation system kicking on. He had stopped cooking with any strong-smelling ingredients, because the scent of onions or garlic sometimes triggered a wave of olfactory recall that left him shaking. He had stopped visiting his daughter's house, because her apartment building had a faint, clean smell he could not identify, and he could not bear to ask about it.

What finally brought Richard to seek help was a morning when he found himself standing in his own bathroom, staring at the shower curtain, unable to remember how he had gotten there. He had been thinking about the hotel, about whether he would ever be able to return, and then he was somewhere else entirely, his heart racing, his hands cold, and no image in his mind at all. He realized then that he was not getting better on his own. He was afraid of what might happen if he did not find a way to stop this—afraid that he would lose his job, his apartment, his connection to his daughter. But he was equally afraid of what it would mean to talk about it, to open the door to that memory and let it fully in. He hoped, more than anything, that someone could help him feel safe in his own body again, though he did not know if that was possible.
